newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New Russian cabinet gets to work amid rivalries.
newsitem.headline: New Russian cabinet gets to work amid rivalries.

text.p: Russia's new administration is setting its sights on how to revive a devastated economy, but the task is being complicated by rivalries between promoted liberals and an old guard which some opponents say spell crisis.

Exactly a month after President Boris Yeltsin returned from his long illness and ordered a sweeping cabinet shake-up to break a downward national spiral of poverty and corruption, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Sunday that the new team was nearly complete and united behind its reforming goals.

"I am sure we have a realistic chance of a breakthrough in the economic situation this year," the premier told Moskovsky Komsomolets newspaper and RIA news agency, adding that there were still a few more personnel changes pending.

But Kremlin and government sources describe bitter in-fighting behind the scenes since Yeltsin named youthful liberals Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov as Chernomyrdin's first deputies last month and promoted other reformers.

It bubbled to the surface last week when Yeltsin backed out of a merger with its barely reformed ex-Soviet neighbour Belarus and, much to the irritation of hardline President Alexander Lukashenko, signed only a much watered down Union Treaty.
Kremlin sources said Chubais, 41, led a last-minute campaign against the original plan. Analysts called it a first major victory in what they see as a long-running war.

Yeltsin, in radio address on Saturday, criticised "some politicians" for trying to railroad through the Belarus merger and, echoing the concerns of the liberals, added that Moscow would not sacrifice economic and political reforms for union with Minsk.
On Friday, he sacked foreign policy adviser Dmitry Ryurikov. Kremlin sources said he pushed the Belarus merger too hard.

Some Russian commentators say the administration is increasingly divided along lines not seen since tsarist times, between liberal "Westerners", who look to foreign models, and more conservative "Slavophiles", who backed the Belarus union.

Chernomyrdin said on Sunday differences of opinion simply reflected healthy cabinet discussion. In angrily denying media reports he had amassed a personal fortune, however, he accused unnamed rivals of promoting a smear campaign against him.

Some government sources say the new cabinet is not a happy family. One promoted liberal told Reuters privately that a conservative colleague had tried, though failed, to block his attempts to appoint new senior staff in his own department.
Grigory Yavlinsky, leader of the opposition liberal party Yabloko, said at the weekend that the new reformers would be unable to break the grip of big business on the government.
Yavlinsky has long accused Chernomyrdin, former head of the Gazprom gas monopoly, of putting commercial interests first.

The liberal leader said the cabinet was riven by faction fighting among three powerful lobbies -- the big banks, oil and gas groups and the arms industry -- and warned of a summer economic crisis that would play into the hands of the communist opposition and might prompt Yeltsin to dismiss the government.
Naturally ministers are more optimistic. But liberal Deputy Prime Minister Alfred Kokh said on Saturday that a 42 percent shortfall in tax collection posed a "crisis of statehood".
The head of the state tax service was reported to have tendered his resignation to Chernomyrdin at the weekend.

Nemtsov, charged by Yeltsin with getting monopolies under control, said at the weekend the president would sign decrees introducing competition in bidding for federal contracts and regulating how the state gives business to commercial banks.
Nemtsov, who has decribed his anti-trust role as political "suicide", said on Friday the state should reassert authority over Gazprom, give it competition and make it pay its taxes.
Energy Minister Pyotr Rodionov resigned on Friday -- he may return to wealthy former employer Gazprom -- adding to the appointments Chernomyrdin says he must still make.
After a string of liberal newcomers to influential posts, analysts will be watching the new names closely for more clues to the future complexion of the administration.
